Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Ordinarily, adults (aged 15 years and older) take 1 sachet (a single dose) at a time; those aged 11 years and older but under 15 years take 2/3 sachet (2/3 of the adult single dose) at a time; and those aged 7 years and older but under 11 years take 1/2 sachet (1/2 of the adult single dose) at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Serious skin reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), which can very rarely be fatal, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • This medicine contains aspartame, which is metabolized to phenylalanine in the body, so patients with phenylketonuria who need to restrict their phenylalanine intake must not take it.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, those who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants (nursing infants) under 3 months of age, patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption, and patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure must not take this medicine.

  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia; rarely shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling (puffiness), and chest tightness right after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing); Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome); toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness and blistering like burns appearing on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes); asthma; liver function disorder (general lethargy, jaundice, etc.); interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.); pseudoaldosteronism (decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands, and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, raised blood pressure or headache, etc.); or myopathy (weakness, cramping of the limbs, paralysis).

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussives and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness remedies, antiallergic remedies).

How to take it

For the first doses, adults take 30 mL (20 g) once a day with breakfast or dinner, and in most patients, several days after the initial administration, the maintenance dose is 15 mL (10 g) once a day. The average dose for children is 0.375 mL (0.25 g) per kg of body weight per day: children aged 1 to 6 years take 3.75 to 7.5 mL (2.5 to 5 g) a day, children aged 6 to 12 years take 7.5 to 15 mL (5 to 10 g) a day, and those aged 12 to 16 years take 15 to 30 mL (10 to 20 g) a day. Because the response varies from patient to patient, for patients with constipation the dose needs to be adjusted to the amount required for one bowel movement a day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, intestinal obstruction (blocked bowel), abdominal pain or bleeding of unknown cause, fecal impaction, galactosemia, an ileal or rectal incision, inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, etc.), or a colostomy, and nursing mothers must not take this medicine.

  • If constipation does not improve after taking it for about 1 week, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • If abdominal (belly) discomfort such as flatulence, pain, abdominal pain (stomach ache), cramps, or a feeling of fullness in the abdomen, rarely vomiting, occasionally nausea, borborygmus (the sound of gas in the intestines) or anal itching, diarrhea, an increased number of bowel movements, loss of appetite, itching, elevated LDH, decreased hemoglobin, eosinophilia, or malaise occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

Adults aged 15 years and older take 2 capsules as 1 dose, and those over 7 years and under 15 years take 1 capsule as 1 dose, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.

  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you are an infant or a child under 15 years of age who is infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, a child under 2 years of age, have an allergic constitution, have experienced allergic symptoms (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), have liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, or a gastroduodenal ulcer, are elderly, are physically weak or have a high fever, have persistent or recurring stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain, or have ulcer or bleeding problems, are pregnant or may be pregnant or are breastfeeding, or have smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough with excessive phlegm, a cough that persists or recurs for 1 week or longer, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or a persistent headache.

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinson drugs, etc.), antitussives and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral medicines for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, medicines for allergies).

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), fever and pain due to a cold, low back pain, dysmenorrhea, post-operative pain and ankylosing spondylitis, headache, toothache, muscle pain, neuralgia, acute gout, psoriatic arthritis, soft tissue injury (sprain, contusion), and non-articular rheumatic diseases (tendinitis, tenosynovitis, bursitis).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint diseas

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199302363. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be taken. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight per dose, in 3 to 4 divided doses a day. For mild to moderate pain and for colds, adults take 200 to 400 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased as appropriate according to age and symptoms. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 12.5 mL) per dose, those aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 mL) per dose, those aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 mL) per dose, and those aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 mL) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day, and it is advisable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years may take up to 1,000 mg (50 mL) a day, those aged 7 to 10 years up to 800 mg (40 mL), those aged 3 to 6 years up to 600 mg (30 mL), and those aged 1 to 2 years up to 400 mg (20 mL).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood abnormalities, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, patients who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, breastfeeding women, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Do not take more than the recommended dose.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, heart disease, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, pregnant women, and patients with chickenpox should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • When taking it for a cold, take it for no more than 5 days as a rule, and without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

Possible side effects

  • If shock (difficulty breathing, fall in blood pressure, etc.), blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function or eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, vomiting of blood, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal distension, oral ulcers, constipation, black stools, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, hepatitis, jaundice, abnormal liver function, liver disorder, hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purple spots, visual disturbance, deafness, ringing in the ears, taste abnormality, vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever or impaired consciousness), acute renal failure, decreased urination, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN or blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath or listlessness, Kounis syndrome of unknown frequency, swelling around the eyes, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed, swelling or peripheral edema appear, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy should not take this medicine, and do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • Before taking this medicine, people taking low-dose aspirin or ACE inhibitors and patients taking lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Who should ask first

How to take it

Those 15 years and older and adults take 2 capsules at a time, and those 7 years and older but under 15 years take 1 capsule at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.

  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, children under 2 years of age, people with an allergic constitution, people who have experienced allergic symptoms (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), or difficulty urinating (passing urine), elderly people, people who are physically weak or who have a high fever, people with persistent or recurring gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, people with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that persists or recurs for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or a persistent headache, and patients hypersensitive to Yellow No. 5 or with such a history should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after 5 to 6 doses, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, rarely shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling and tightness in the chest immediately after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweats and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, in which rash and redness and blisters like burns appear on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), asthma, liver function disorder (listlessness of the whole body, jaundice), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, breathlessness, difficulty breathing and fever), a decrease in urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, a rise in blood pressure, headache, myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis) or the like occurs, stop taking the medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussive-expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness remedies, anti-allergy remedies).
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants or alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics, or thiazide diuretics.

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendinitis, acute gout, dysmenorrhea and bursitis, skeletal muscle disorders (sprain, contusion (bruise), trauma (wound), lumbosacral pain (low back pain)), postoperative pain (aches), migraine, and pain after tooth extraction (pulling out a tooth).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendini

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199902599. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, adults take 1 to 2 tablets (275 to 550 mg) at a time, twice a day (every 12 hours). For acute gout, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 8 hours until the attack subsides. For skeletal muscle disorders, pain after surgery, pain after tooth extraction (having a tooth pulled), dysmenorrhea, tendinitis (inflammation of a tendon), and bursitis (inflammation of the lubricating sac), take 2 tablets (550 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 6 to 8 hours, and do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg). For migraine, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose); if necessary, 1 to 2 more tablets (275 to 550 mg) may be taken a day, and these are taken 30 minutes after the initial dose (the first dose). Do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe renal disorder or severe high blood pressure, patients hypersensitive to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as aspirin, patients who have had asthma, rhinitis (nasal inflammation), nasal polyps, urticaria or an allergic reaction caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors) or those who have experienced them, patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and children aged 2 years or under must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, children, the elderly, those who have experienced peptic ulcer, those who have experienced blood abnormalities, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with liver disorder or those who have experienced it, patients with renal disorder or those who have experienced it, and patients with cardiac dysfunction, high blood pressure, bronchial asthma, systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If an increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke, serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions that may be fatal such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcers, and perforation, rarely shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, a fall in blood pressure, bradycardia (a slow pulse), cold sweat, swelling), PIE syndrome (pulmonary infiltration with eosinophilia: accompanied by fever, wheezing, coughing, and phlegm), urticaria, occasionally hypersensitivity symptoms such as rash or itching, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness), eczema, sweating, purpura (purple spots), photosensitivity, hair loss, redness (turning red from congestion), necrolysis, erythema multiforme (red spots of various shapes), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), urticaria, epidermolysis bullosa, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, fixed drug eruption, exfoliative dermatitis, or rarely blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic (red-blood-cell-destroying) anemia, or reduced platelet function (prolongation of bleeding time) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Occasionally stomach discomfort, stomach pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, or stomatitis (inflammation inside the mouth), and rarely abdominal bloating, black stools, dry mouth, elevated GOT and GPT values, jaundice, hepatitis, kidney disorder, nephritis, hematuria, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, proteinuria (urine containing protein), renal failure, ringing in the ears, hearing impairment, visual impairment, swelling, difficulty breathing, palpitations (a pounding heart), myasthenia (muscle weakness), congestive heart failure, eosinophilic pneumonia, anaphylactoid reactions, menstrual disorders, chills (feeling cold and shivering) and fever, vasculitis, high blood sugar, or low blood sugar may occur.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics or naproxen derivatives, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with hydantoin antiepileptics, sulfonamides, sulfonylurea hypoglycemic agents, propranolol and other blockers, ACE inhibitors (such as captopril), loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics, probenecid, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (blood-clotting inhibitors) (such as warfarin), zidovudine, or new quinolone antibiotics (such as enoxacin).

Oral medicine (MFDS 201802134)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201802134. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, cough, phlegm, chills (feeling cold and shivering), fever, headache, joint pain, muscle pain).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, co

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201802134. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over take 24 mL (2 sachets) at a time, those aged 11 years and over but under 15 years take 16 mL (1 and 1/3 sachets) at a time, those aged 7 years and over but under 11 years take 12 mL (1 sachet) at a time, those aged 3 years and over but under 7 years take 8 mL (2/3 sachet) at a time, and those aged 2 years and over but under 3 years take 6 mL (1/2 sachet) at a time, three times a day, 30 minutes after meals. If necessary it may be taken at bedtime, and as a rule the interval between doses should be 4 hours.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Those with hypersensitivity to this medicine or who have experienced it, those who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age, breastfeeding women, and people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) or who stopped taking them within the past 2 weeks must not take this medicine.Before taking this medicine, infants infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza and children under 15 years of age, infants and young children aged 3 months and older but under 2 years, those with an allergic constitution, those who have experienced allergic symptoms (e.g. fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), those with liver, kidney, heart, or thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, edema, or gastroduodenal ulcer, elderly people, physically weak people or people with a high fever, people with persistent or recurring gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, gastric discomfort, or stomach pain or with ulcer or bleeding problems, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant, and people who smoke or have asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough persisting or recurring for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever and rash or persistent headache should consult a doctor or pharmacist.Strictly observe the specified dosage and administration.When administering to children, do so under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.Do not take it continuously over a long period.Do not drink alcohol while taking it.Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so be careful when driving or operating machinery.If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it about 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness (congested and reddened skin), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema (swelling), difficulty urinating (passing urine), thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling (puffiness) and tightness in the chest immediately after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweats and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome: severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, such as rash and redness and blisters like burns), asthma, listlessness of the whole body, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes taking on a yellow color), coughing with breathlessness, difficulty breathing, fever or the like occurs, stop taking the medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other products containing acetaminophen, MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinson drugs, etc.), antitussives (which stop coughing) and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • Patients who have taken diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants or alcohol should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults take 1 bottle per dose, 1 time a day.

Warning

  • Since it is manufactured using human placenta as a raw material, take it only when its benefits outweigh its risks.

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectoration in diseases such as acute and chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma, laryngitis, sinusitis, and cystic fibrosis.

Category

How it works

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectoration in diseases such as acute and chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201206670. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For acute conditions, adults take 200 mg at a time 3 times a day, those aged 6 to 14 years take 200 mg at a time twice a day, and those aged 2 to 5 years take 100 mg at a time 3 times a day, all before meals. For chronic conditions, adults take 200 mg at a time twice a day and those aged 6 to 14 years take 100 mg at a time 3 times a day, before meals. For cystic fibrosis, those aged 6 years and over take 200 mg at a time 3 times a day and those aged 2 to 5 years take 100 mg at a time 4 times a day, before meals.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with gastric or duodenal ulcer, and infants under 2 years of age must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If, rarely, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, heartburn, diarrhea, urticaria, itching, rash, headache, tinnitus, bronchospasm (especially in asthma patients), tachycardia, hypertension, or the like appear, stop this administration immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • When taking this medicine together with oral antibiotics (amoxicillin, cefuroxime, doxycycline, erythromycin, thiamphenicol), leave an interval of at least 2 hours between doses.Avoid adding other medicines to the solution of this medicine.

How it works

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202004020. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults take 4 tablets at a time, 3 times a day, before meals or between meals.

Precautions for use

  • Pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and nursing mothers, and patients with genetic problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, elderly people, patients with high blood pressure, heart disorder or kidney disorder, edema, or a weak stomach and intestines, patients with symptoms of diarrhea, loose stools, loss of appetite, nausea, or vomiting, patients in a weakened state after illness or whose physical strength is markedly weakened, patients who sweat a great deal, patients with circulatory disorders such as angina or myocardial infarction, urination disorders, hyperthyroidism, or diabetes, and those who have experienced allergic symptoms (rash, redness, itching, etc.) should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not take it continuously for 1 week or longer.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it for about 1 month (about 1 week when it is taken for constipation), stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, rising blood pressure or headache, myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis), loss of appetite, stomach discomfort, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, rash, redness, itching, insomnia, excessive sweating, rapid pulse, frequent urination, palpitations, general weakness, mental excitement, difficulty urinating, jaundice, or liver function disorder accompanied by elevations of AST, ALT, ALP, or γ-GTP occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take together with other laxatives.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with preparations containing ephedra or ephedrine, MAO inhibitors, thyroid preparations (thyroxine, liothyronine), catecholamine preparations (epinephrine, isoprenaline), xanthine preparations (theophylline, diprophylline), potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid), or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide).

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendinitis, acute gout, dysmenorrhea and bursitis, skeletal muscle disorders (sprain, contusion (bruise), trauma (wound), lumbosacral pain (low back pain)), postoperative pain (aches), migraine, and pain after tooth extraction (pulling out a tooth).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendini

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199902599. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, adults take 1 to 2 tablets (275 to 550 mg) at a time, twice a day (every 12 hours). For acute gout, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 8 hours until the attack subsides. For skeletal muscle disorders, pain after surgery, pain after tooth extraction (having a tooth pulled), dysmenorrhea, tendinitis (inflammation of a tendon), and bursitis (inflammation of the lubricating sac), take 2 tablets (550 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 6 to 8 hours, and do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg). For migraine, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose); if necessary, 1 to 2 more tablets (275 to 550 mg) may be taken a day, and these are taken 30 minutes after the initial dose (the first dose). Do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe renal disorder or severe high blood pressure, patients hypersensitive to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as aspirin, patients who have had asthma, rhinitis (nasal inflammation), nasal polyps, urticaria or an allergic reaction caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors) or those who have experienced them, patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and children aged 2 years or under must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, children, the elderly, those who have experienced peptic ulcer, those who have experienced blood abnormalities, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with liver disorder or those who have experienced it, patients with renal disorder or those who have experienced it, and patients with cardiac dysfunction, high blood pressure, bronchial asthma, systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If an increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke, serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions that may be fatal such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcers, and perforation, rarely shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, a fall in blood pressure, bradycardia (a slow pulse), cold sweat, swelling), PIE syndrome (pulmonary infiltration with eosinophilia: accompanied by fever, wheezing, coughing, and phlegm), urticaria, occasionally hypersensitivity symptoms such as rash or itching, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness), eczema, sweating, purpura (purple spots), photosensitivity, hair loss, redness (turning red from congestion), necrolysis, erythema multiforme (red spots of various shapes), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), urticaria, epidermolysis bullosa, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, fixed drug eruption, exfoliative dermatitis, or rarely blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic (red-blood-cell-destroying) anemia, or reduced platelet function (prolongation of bleeding time) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Occasionally stomach discomfort, stomach pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, or stomatitis (inflammation inside the mouth), and rarely abdominal bloating, black stools, dry mouth, elevated GOT and GPT values, jaundice, hepatitis, kidney disorder, nephritis, hematuria, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, proteinuria (urine containing protein), renal failure, ringing in the ears, hearing impairment, visual impairment, swelling, difficulty breathing, palpitations (a pounding heart), myasthenia (muscle weakness), congestive heart failure, eosinophilic pneumonia, anaphylactoid reactions, menstrual disorders, chills (feeling cold and shivering) and fever, vasculitis, high blood sugar, or low blood sugar may occur.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics or naproxen derivatives, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with hydantoin antiepileptics, sulfonamides, sulfonylurea hypoglycemic agents, propranolol and other blockers, ACE inhibitors (such as captopril), loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics, probenecid, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (blood-clotting inhibitors) (such as warfarin), zidovudine, or new quinolone antibiotics (such as enoxacin).

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.

  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, those who have experienced asthma when taking this medicine or its ingredients, other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants (nursing infants, newborns) under 3 months of age, people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinson drugs, etc.) or are within 2 weeks of stopping them, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.

  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rash and redness (reddening of the skin), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling (puffiness), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia; rarely shock (urticaria, swelling (puffiness), and chest tightness right after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, difficulty breathing, etc.); Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome); toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome); asthma; liver function disorder (general lethargy, jaundice, etc.); interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.); pseudoaldosteronism (decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands, and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, raised blood pressure or headache, etc.); or myopathy (muscle disease) (weakness, cramping of the limbs, paralysis, etc.).

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussives (which stop coughing) and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis (nasal inflammation), motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).If taking it together with antidiabetic medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants and alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid), or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide), consult a doctor or pharmacist.Do not drink alcohol when taking it.

Oral medicine (MFDS 200101057)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200101057. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used for cough, phlegm, and hoarseness of the throat, pain and swelling of the throat, and throat discomfort caused by inflammation of the throat.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for cough, phlegm, and hoarseness of the throat, pain and swelling of the throat, and throat disco

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200101057. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults and adolescents aged 15 years and older take 1 sachet as 1 dose, those aged 11 years or older and under 15 years take 2/3 of a sachet as 1 dose, those aged 7 years or older and under 11 years take 1/2 of a sachet as 1 dose, and those aged 3 years or older and under 7 years take 1/3 of a sachet as 1 dose, 3 to 6 times a day without water. The interval between doses should be 2 hours or more.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant, people who are taking an MAO inhibitor (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian drugs, etc.) or who stopped taking one within the past 2 weeks, children under 3 years of age, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine (applies to the mint flavor).
  • Before taking this medicine, people with an allergic constitution, people who have experienced allergic symptoms from medicines (e.g., fever, rash, joint pain, itching, etc.), patients with diseases such as liver disease, kidney disease, thyroid disease, or diabetes, patients with a high fever, frail people, patients with heart disease and high blood pressure, elderly people, breastfeeding women, patients with edema (swelling), patients with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, or emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that lasts 1 week or more or recurs, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or persistent headache, and people who have experienced hypersensitivity or an allergic reaction to Yellow No. 5 (applies to the mint flavor and the mint coffee flavor) should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after 5 to 6 doses, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration exactly.
  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.

Possible side effects

  • If rash, redness (congested and reddened skin), itching, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dizziness, decreased urine volume, swelling of the face and limbs, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, increased blood pressure, headache, weakness, cramps in the limbs, or paralysis occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take together with other antitussives and expectorants, cold remedies, antihistamines, sedatives, or alcohol.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you use it together with potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid), or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide).
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

This medicine is used to supply B2 and B6 during physical fatigue, pregnancy and breastfeeding, and reduced physical strength during or after illness, to relieve the symptoms of angular cheilitis (inflammation of the corners of the mouth), cheilitis (inflammation of the lips), stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth), glossitis (inflammation of the tongue), eczema, and dermatitis, and for muscle cramps caused by magnesium deficiency.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to supply B2 and B6 during physical fatigue, pregnancy and breastfeeding, and reduced physical str

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202007806. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults and those aged 12 years and older take 1 dose of 20 mL, 2 times a day, between meals (in between mealtimes).

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, infants under 12 months of age, and patients with severe renal (kidney) failure must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, nursing mothers, premature infants, young children, patients with cardiac and circulatory dysfunction, kidney (renal) disorder, or hypoproteinemia, and patients with hypersensitivity to caramel should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • It may turn the urine yellow and affect clinical laboratory test values.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it for about 1 month, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If red spots, diarrhea, asystole (stopping of the heartbeat), decreased central nervous system function, gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea and vomiting, hypernatremia, congestive heart failure, or edema (swelling) occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take it together with phosphates, calcium salts, oral tetracycline preparations, antacids or levodopa.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with an antialdosterone agent or triamterene.
  • Avoid tea containing tannin, such as green tea and black tea, while taking it and before and after taking it.

This medicine is used for fever and pain (aches) caused by a cold, headache, neuralgia, muscle pain, menstrual pain, sprain pain (pain from a sprain), toothache, joint pain, and rheumatic pain (aches)

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for fever and pain (aches) caused by a cold, headache, neuralgia, muscle pain, menstrual pain, spr

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202202278. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 12 years or younger take the recommended single dose every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Take this medicine at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible period, and do not take more than 5 doses in 1 day (75 mg/kg). If the body weight is known, it is more appropriate to dose according to body weight (10 to 15 mg/kg). Refer to the approved labeling for doses by age group.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, hepatic impairment, kidney (renal) impairment, or reduced cardiac function, patients with aspirin-induced asthma (induction of asthma attacks by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) or those who have experienced it, and people who have taken barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with hepatic impairment, kidney (renal) impairment, peptic ulcer, or blood abnormalities or those who have experienced them, patients with a bleeding tendency or cardiac dysfunction, people who have experienced hypersensitivity, patients with bronchial asthma, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, and pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If shock, anaphylactoid symptoms (difficulty breathing, reddening of the whole body, angioedema, urticaria, etc.), asthma attacks, thrombocytopenia, granulocytopenia, hemolytic anemia (destruction of red blood cells), methemoglobinemia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), cyanosis, hypersensitivity symptoms (facial swelling, difficulty breathing, sweating, low blood pressure, shock), nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer and perforation with long-term use, rash, allergic reactions, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), elevated AST, elevated ALT, or fixed drug eruption occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine together with warfarin, lithium, or thiazide diuretics.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, co

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201902788. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over and adults take 2 capsules at a time, and those over 7 years but under 15 years take 1 capsule at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious and potentially fatal skin reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If a severe skin adverse reaction such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occurs, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine or those who have experienced it, those who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants (newborns) under 3 months of age, and patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, the following should consult a doctor or pharmacist: infants (newborns) and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; children under 2 years of age; those in whom symptoms of ischemic colitis (sudden abdominal pain (stomach ache), rectal bleeding, etc.) appear; people with an allergic constitution or who have experienced allergic symptoms (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.); people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.) or difficulty urinating; the elderly; people with a weak body or a high fever; people with persistent or recurrent stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems; pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women; and patients with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough with excessive phlegm, a cough lasting or recurring for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash or persistent headache.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rash and redness (reddening of the skin), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling (puffiness), difficulty urinating (passing urine), thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia; rarely shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling (puffiness), and chest tightness right after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing); Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome); toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness and blistering like burns appearing on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes); acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, fever, erythema (red spots), numerous small pustules; asthma; liver function disorder (general lethargy, jaundice); or interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever).
  • If symptoms of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, visual disturbances, etc.) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinson drugs, etc.), antitussives (which stop coughing) and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis (nasal inflammation), motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • People who are within 2 weeks of stopping MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinson drugs, etc.) must not take this medicine.
  • If taken together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants or alcohol, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

How it works

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202108189. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults usually take 4 tablets at a time, 3 times a day, before meals or between meals.

Precautions for use

  • People who have hypersensitivity to the soybean oil in this medicine or who have experienced allergic reactions to it, patients with hypersensitivity to soybeans or peanuts, women who are pregnant or may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with high blood pressure, patients with heart disorder or kidney disorder, edema, elderly people, patients with symptoms of diarrhea or loose stools, patients with a weak stomach and intestines, patients with symptoms of loss of appetite, nausea, or vomiting, patients in a weakened state after illness, patients whose physical strength is markedly weakened, patients who sweat a great deal, patients with circulatory disorders such as angina or myocardial infarction or a history of them, patients with urination disorders or hyperthyroidism, people who have experienced rash, redness, or itching from this medicine, and patients with diabetes or with disorders of fat metabolism such as hyperlipoproteinemia, diabetic hyperlipidemia, and pancreatitis, or patients who must be given lipid emulsions with caution, should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it for about 1 month (1 week when taking it for constipation), stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the specified dosage and administration carefully.

Possible side effects

  • If pseudoaldosteronism (a decrease in urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, a rise in blood pressure, headache, etc.), myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis), loss of appetite, stomach discomfort, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, rash and redness, itching, insomnia, excessive sweating, a rapid pulse, frequent urination, palpitations, generalized weakness, mental excitement, urinary difficulty, or liver function disorder accompanied by elevated AST, ALT, ALP or -GTP (generalized listlessness, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turning yellow)) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other laxatives.
  • When taking it in combination with other herbal (crude drug) preparations, take care not to duplicate the crude drugs they contain.
  • Take it with caution when combined with preparations containing ephedra or ephedrine, MAO inhibitors, thyroid preparations (thyroxine, liothyronine), catecholamine preparations (epinephrine, isoprenaline), xanthine preparations (theophylline, diprophylline), potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid) or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide).

This medicine is used for the relief of the various symptoms of the common cold (sore throat (pain in the throat), chills (feeling cold and shivering), fever, headache, joint pain, muscle pain).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for the relief of the various symptoms of the common cold (sore throat (pain in the throat), chill

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201900992. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over and adults take 1 packet (a single dose) at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. The interval between doses should be 4 hours.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants (babies) under 3 months of age, and people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) or are within 2 weeks of having stopped them must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants and children under 15 years of age who have or are suspected of having a chickenpox or influenza infection, people with an allergic constitution, people who have experienced allergic symptoms (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, edema (swelling), gastroduodenal ulcer and the like, the elderly, people with a weak body or a high fever, people with persistent or recurring stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach (upper abdominal) discomfort or stomach pain, or with ulcer or bleeding problems, women who are pregnant or may be pregnant, breastfeeding women, and children under 2 years of age should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling (puffiness), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia; rarely shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling (puffiness), and chest tightness right after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing); Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome); toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness (reddening of the skin) and blistering like burns appearing on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes); asthma; liver function disorder (general lethargy, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turn yellow)); interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever); pseudoaldosteronism; or myopathy (muscle disease).

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with antitussives (which stop coughing) and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis (nasal inflammation), motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • If it is taken together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid), or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide), consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.

How it works

This medicine is used to prevent and relieve dizziness, vomiting, and headache caused by motion sickness.

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202400578. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over take 1/2 sachet (15 ml) at a time, those aged 11 years and over but under 15 years take 1 sachet (10 ml) at a time, those aged 7 years and over but under 11 years take 3/4 sachet (7.5 ml) at a time, and those aged 3 years and over but under 7 years take 1/2 sachet (5 ml) at a time; for the prevention of motion sickness, take it 30 minutes before boarding a vehicle or vessel. If an additional dose is needed, take one dose leaving an interval of at least 4 hours. Limit the number of doses to 3 times a day.

Precautions for use

  • Breastfeeding women and infants and young children under 3 years of age must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, people who have experienced allergic symptoms such as rash, congestion causing reddening, or itching from medicines, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant, breastfeeding women, patients with glaucoma, patients with urinary disorders, and patients with respiratory diseases such as emphysema or chronic bronchitis should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If you divide 1 sachet and take the remainder later, seal the opening well, store it, and take it within 2 days.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • When administering it to children, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.

Possible side effects

  • If rash, redness from congestion, itching, or thirst occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take other antiemetics, cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, antihistamines, sedatives, or antitussive-expectorants.
  • Do not drink alcoholic beverages while taking this medicine.

payloads.content:

Oral medicine (MFDS 201305834)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201305834. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This drug is used for reducing fever when fever occurs due to acute upper respiratory tract infection.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This drug is used for reducing fever when fever occurs due to acute upper respiratory tract infection.

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201305834. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 6 months and over take 0.4 to 0.6 mL/kg (5 to 7 mg/kg) at a time as needed, at intervals of 4 to 6 hours, not exceeding a maximum of 4 times a day (28 mg/kg). For children weighing 30 kg or less, do not exceed a maximum of 25 mL (300 mg) a day. If the body weight is known it is more appropriate to give the dose based on body weight, so refer to the approved labelling for the recommended doses by age group.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious, potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, or those with a history of these, people who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or an allergic reaction to aspirin or another non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesic (including COX-2 inhibitors), patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, and women who are pregnant or may be pregnant or are breastfeeding must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you have a history of peptic ulcer, blood abnormalities or a history of them, a bleeding tendency (platelet dysfunction may occur), liver disorder or a history of it, kidney disorder or a history of it, cardiac insufficiency, high blood pressure, a history of hypersensitivity, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, are elderly or a child, or have stomach cancer.
  • Considering the importance of the medication, either stop breastfeeding or stop the medication.
  • Dizziness or fatigue may occur after taking this medicine, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • When taking it long term for an acute condition, keep it to within 5 days as a rule.

Possible side effects

  • If shock (difficulty breathing, a drop in blood pressure, etc.), blood disorders such as aplastic anaemia, haemolytic anaemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), or eosinophilia occur, or peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (oculomucocutaneous syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), induction of an asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purpura, occasionally rash or itching, rarely visual disturbances such as loss of vision or scotoma, aseptic meningitis, acute renal failure, oliguria, haematuria, proteinuria, a rise in BUN or blood creatinine, or hyperkalaemia occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Occasionally loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhoea, or stomach discomfort may occur; very rarely thirst, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, or constipation; rarely jaundice, a rise in GOT, GPT, or AL-P, hearing loss, tinnitus, taste disturbance, a drop in blood pressure, a rise in blood pressure, palpitations, reduced urine output, generalised oedema and the accompanying shortness of breath, listlessness, or acute pulmonary oedema; occasionally periorbital oedema; and very rarely malaise, fever, or nosebleed.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with glucocorticoids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, diuretics, antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors, furosemide, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or low-dose aspirin.

This medicine is used for fever and pain caused by colds, headache, neuralgia, muscle pain, menstrual pain, sprain pain, toothache, joint pain, and rheumatic pain.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for fever and pain caused by colds, headache, neuralgia, muscle pain, menstrual pain, sprain pain,

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202005623. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 7 to 12 years take the recommended single dose directly on the tongue without water, every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Take this medicine at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible period, and do not take it more than 5 times a day (75 mg/kg). If the body weight is known, it is more appropriate to take a dose based on body weight (10 to 15 mg/kg). For the doses by age group, refer to the approved product information.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, or severe cardiac dysfunction, and patients with aspirin-induced asthma (asthma attacks triggered by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents) or a history of it must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with liver disorder or a history of it, patients with kidney disorder or a history of it, people who have had peptic ulcer, patients with blood abnormalities or a history of them, patients with a bleeding tendency, cardiac dysfunction, or a history of hypersensitivity, patients with bronchial asthma, elderly people (the aged), children under 2 years of age, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and patients with low glutathione reserves should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist, do not take it for pain for more than 10 days (adults) or more than 5 days (children), and do not take it for fever for more than 3 days.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, reddening of the whole body, angioedema, urticaria, etc.), asthma attacks, thrombocytopenia, granulocytopenia, hemolytic (red blood cell-destroying) anemia, methemoglobinemia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), cyanosis, hypersensitivity symptoms (facial swelling, difficulty breathing, sweating, low blood pressure, shock), nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, gastrointestinal problems with long-term use such as gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, and perforation (a hole), rash, allergic reactions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), elevated AST, elevated ALT, or fixed drug eruption occurs, or if pain or fever persists or worsens, or if new symptoms appear, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol or other anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • If you take it together with warfarin or flucloxacillin, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
