Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202501250. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over take 1 packet (20 mL) at a time, those aged 11 years and over but under 15 years take 2/3 of a packet (13.3 mL) at a time, those aged 7 years and over but under 11 years take 1/2 of a packet (10 mL) at a time, those aged 3 years and over but under 7 years take 1/3 of a packet (6.7 mL), and those aged 2 years and over but under 3 years take 1/4 of a packet (5 mL), 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. In principle the interval between doses should be 4 hours.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take this medicine together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, people who have had an asthma attack when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, children under 2 years of age, and people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinson drugs, etc.) or are within 2 weeks of stopping them must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, people with an allergic constitution, patients with liver, kidney, heart or thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure or gastroduodenal ulcer, the elderly, people with a weak body or a high fever, people with persistent or recurrent stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant, breastfeeding women, and people with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough with excessive phlegm, a cough lasting or recurring for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash or persistent headache should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking this medicine, so take care when driving or operating machinery.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, rarely urticaria, chest tightness with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome: accompanied by high fever, with severe symptoms such as rash and redness and burn-like blistering), asthma, generalized lassitude, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turn yellow), or interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and fever) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other products containing acetaminophen, antitussives and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness remedies, antiallergic remedies).
  • If you have taken antidiabetic drugs, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendinitis, acute gout, dysmenorrhea and bursitis, skeletal muscle disorders (sprain, contusion (bruise), trauma (wound), lumbosacral pain (low back pain)), postoperative pain (aches), migraine, and pain after tooth extraction (pulling out a tooth).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendini

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199902599. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, adults take 1 to 2 tablets (275 to 550 mg) at a time, twice a day (every 12 hours). For acute gout, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 8 hours until the attack subsides. For skeletal muscle disorders, pain after surgery, pain after tooth extraction (having a tooth pulled), dysmenorrhea, tendinitis (inflammation of a tendon), and bursitis (inflammation of the lubricating sac), take 2 tablets (550 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 6 to 8 hours, and do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg). For migraine, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose); if necessary, 1 to 2 more tablets (275 to 550 mg) may be taken a day, and these are taken 30 minutes after the initial dose (the first dose). Do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe renal disorder or severe high blood pressure, patients hypersensitive to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as aspirin, patients who have had asthma, rhinitis (nasal inflammation), nasal polyps, urticaria or an allergic reaction caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors) or those who have experienced them, patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and children aged 2 years or under must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, children, the elderly, those who have experienced peptic ulcer, those who have experienced blood abnormalities, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with liver disorder or those who have experienced it, patients with renal disorder or those who have experienced it, and patients with cardiac dysfunction, high blood pressure, bronchial asthma, systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If an increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke, serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions that may be fatal such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcers, and perforation, rarely shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, a fall in blood pressure, bradycardia (a slow pulse), cold sweat, swelling), PIE syndrome (pulmonary infiltration with eosinophilia: accompanied by fever, wheezing, coughing, and phlegm), urticaria, occasionally hypersensitivity symptoms such as rash or itching, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness), eczema, sweating, purpura (purple spots), photosensitivity, hair loss, redness (turning red from congestion), necrolysis, erythema multiforme (red spots of various shapes), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), urticaria, epidermolysis bullosa, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, fixed drug eruption, exfoliative dermatitis, or rarely blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic (red-blood-cell-destroying) anemia, or reduced platelet function (prolongation of bleeding time) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Occasionally stomach discomfort, stomach pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, or stomatitis (inflammation inside the mouth), and rarely abdominal bloating, black stools, dry mouth, elevated GOT and GPT values, jaundice, hepatitis, kidney disorder, nephritis, hematuria, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, proteinuria (urine containing protein), renal failure, ringing in the ears, hearing impairment, visual impairment, swelling, difficulty breathing, palpitations (a pounding heart), myasthenia (muscle weakness), congestive heart failure, eosinophilic pneumonia, anaphylactoid reactions, menstrual disorders, chills (feeling cold and shivering) and fever, vasculitis, high blood sugar, or low blood sugar may occur.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics or naproxen derivatives, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with hydantoin antiepileptics, sulfonamides, sulfonylurea hypoglycemic agents, propranolol and other blockers, ACE inhibitors (such as captopril), loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics, probenecid, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (blood-clotting inhibitors) (such as warfarin), zidovudine, or new quinolone antibiotics (such as enoxacin).

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.

  • It may cause liver damage.

Precautions for use

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendinitis (inflammation of the tendons), acute gout, dysmenorrhea, bursitis (inflammation of the synovial bursa), skeletal muscle disorders (sprains, contusions (bruises), trauma (wounds), lumbosacral pain (low back pain)), pain after surgery, migraine, and pain after tooth extraction (having a tooth pulled).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, ten

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202402681. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, adults take 1 to 2 packets (250 to 500 mg) per dose, 2 times a day every 12 hours. For acute gout, adults take 3 packets (750 mg) as the first dose and then 1 packet (250 mg) every 8 hours until the attack subsides. For skeletal muscle disorders, pain after surgery, pain after tooth extraction, dysmenorrhea, tendinitis (inflammation of the tendon), and bursitis, adults take 2 packets (500 mg) as the first dose and then 1 packet (250 mg) every 6 to 8 hours. Do not exceed a total daily dose of 5 packets (1,250 mg). For migraine, adults take 3 packets (750 mg) as the first dose. If necessary, an additional 1 to 2 packets (250 to 500 mg) may be taken a day, taken 30 minutes after the first dose. Do not exceed a total daily dose of 5 packets (1,250 mg). Increase or decrease the dose as appropriate according to age and symptoms. Shake the suspension well to mix it before use, then take it.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood disorders, liver disorder, cardiac insufficiency, kidney disorder or high blood pressure, patients with hypersensitivity to the ingredients of this medicine or to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as aspirin, those who have experienced asthma, rhinitis, nasal polyps, urticaria or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, and pregnant women (in late pregnancy) must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer or blood disorders or those who have experienced them, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with liver disorder or a history of it, patients with kidney disorder or a history of it and patients with reduced renal blood flow, patients with impaired cardiac function, patients with high blood pressure, those who have experienced hypersensitivity, patients with bronchial asthma, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and patients with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), and elderly people should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • If any of the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely, shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, bradycardia (slow pulse), cold sweat, swelling, etc.), PIE syndrome (pulmonary infiltration with eosinophilia: accompanied by fever, wheezing, cough and sputum), hives; sometimes rash, itching; rarely hematemesis (vomiting of blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation; sometimes stomach discomfort, stomach pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth); rarely abdominal bloating, black stools, thirst; rarely blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, eosinophilia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia (destruction of red blood cells), reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time); rarely elevated GOT and GPT values, jaundice, hepatitis; rarely renal impairment (kidney disorder), glomerulonephritis (kidney inflammation), blood in the urine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis (kidney inflammation), nephrotic syndrome, renal (kidney) papillary necrosis, protein in the urine, renal failure; rarely aseptic meningitis, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness; sometimes drowsiness, impaired cognitive function; rarely dizziness, headache, numbness of the hands and feet, decreased vitality, fatigue, depression, abnormal dreams, loss of concentration, disorientation (impaired orientation), insomnia, muscle pain, muscle weakness; sometimes eczema, sweating, purpura; rarely photosensitivity, hair loss, redness (congested and reddened), necrolysis, erythema multiforme (red spots), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (skin-mucosa-eye syndrome), hives, epidermolysis bullosa, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, fixed drug eruption, ringing in the ears, hearing impairment, visual impairment; Interactions

  • Do not take together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (NSAIDs) or naproxen derivatives.

How to take it

People aged 15 years and over and adults take 2 capsules per dose, 3 times a day, within 30 minutes after a meal.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.

  • Do not take it together with other products that contain acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients who have or have had hypersensitivity to this medicine, by people who have had an asthma attack after taking this medicine, another antipyretic analgesic or a cold remedy, by children under 2 years of age and infants under 3 months of age, or by patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

  • If the symptoms do not improve after 5 to 6 doses, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed directions and amounts.
  • When it is given to a child, give it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Because drowsiness may appear after taking it, take care when driving or operating machinery.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia or high anion gap metabolic acidosis appears, if symptoms of shock rarely appear (urticaria, swelling and a feeling of tightness in the chest right after taking it, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat and difficulty breathing), or if asthma, generalized languor, jaundice, interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.), pseudoaldosteronism (reduced urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heavy eyelids, stiffening of the hands, a rise in blood pressure or headache, etc.) or myopathy (languor, cramp of the limbs, paralysis) appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take it together with antitussives (medicines that stop coughing) and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, oral medicines containing an antihistamine (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, allergy medicines), or flucloxacillin.

Who should ask first

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and older take 1 sachet (20 ml) at a time; those aged 11 years and older but under 15 years take 2/3 sachet at a time; those aged 7 years and older but under 11 years take 1/2 sachet at a time; those aged 3 years and older but under 7 years take 1/3 sachet at a time; and those aged 2 years and older but under 3 years take 1/4 sachet at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious and potentially fatal skin reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of hypersensitivity appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take this medicine together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If a severe skin adverse reaction such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occurs, stop taking this medicine and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine or those who have experienced it, those who have experienced asthma when taking this medicine or its ingredients, other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants under 3 months of age and children under 2 years of age, patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure, and women from 30 weeks of pregnancy onwards must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, the following should consult a doctor or pharmacist: children under 2 years of age when it is absolutely necessary; infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; people with an allergic constitution; pregnant women or women who may be pregnant; breastfeeding women; those in whom symptoms of ischemic colitis such as sudden abdominal pain or rectal bleeding appear in relation to the pseudoephedrine component; those who have experienced allergic symptoms to a medicine such as fever, rash, joint pain, asthma or itching; the elderly; and people with a weak body or a high fever.
  • Before taking this medicine, people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma or difficulty urinating, people with persistent or recurrent stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems, and people with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough with excessive phlegm, a cough lasting or recurring for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash or persistent headache should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If the symptoms do not improve after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Children should take it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • Drowsiness may occur while taking it.
  • Avoid driving a car or operating machinery.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, or insomnia occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • While taking this medicine, do not take antitussives and expectorants, other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives or oral medicines containing an antihistamine.

This medicine is used to relieve all the symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, cough, phlegm, chills, fever, headache, joint pain, muscle pain).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to relieve all the symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, cough,

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201804157. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and older take 20 mL per dose, those aged 11 years to under 15 years take 13.3 mL per dose, those aged 7 years to under 11 years take 10 mL per dose, those aged 3 years to under 7 years take 6.7 mL per dose, and those aged 1 year to under 3 years take 5 mL per dose, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. If necessary, take it at bedtime, and as a rule keep the interval between doses at 4 hours.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of hypersensitivity appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, those who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, and infants under 3 months of age must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, children under 2 years of age, people with an allergic constitution, those who have experienced allergic symptoms (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, edema, gastric and duodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.) or difficulty urinating, elderly people, people with a weak constitution or a high fever, people with persistent or recurring stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort and stomach pain or with ulcers or bleeding problems, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, and patients with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, cough with excessive phlegm, cough lasting or recurring for 1 week or more, chronic cough, or cough accompanied by fever, rash or persistent headache should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking about 5 to 6 doses, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • When giving this medicine to children, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, rarely shock (urticaria, swelling, and chest tightness immediately after taking the medicine together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweats, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) (severe symptoms with high fever, rash and redness, and burn-like blisters appearing on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), asthma, liver function disorder (general listlessness, jaundice), interstitial pneumonia (with cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever), pseudoaldosteronism (decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, rising blood pressure, headache, etc.), or myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis, etc.) occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian drugs, etc.), antitussives and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • If you are taking diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid), or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide), consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

Those aged 15 years and older take 1 sachet (20 ml) at a time; those aged 11 years and older but under 15 years take 2/3 sachet at a time; those aged 7 years and older but under 11 years take 1/2 sachet at a time; those aged 3 years and older but under 7 years take 1/3 sachet at a time; and those aged 2 years and older but under 3 years take 1/4 sachet at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious and potentially fatal skin reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of hypersensitivity appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take this medicine together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If a severe skin adverse reaction such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occurs, stop taking this medicine and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine or those who have experienced it, those who have experienced asthma when taking this medicine or its ingredients, other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants under 3 months of age and children under 2 years of age, patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure, and women from 30 weeks of pregnancy onwards must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, the following should consult a doctor or pharmacist: children under 2 years of age when it is absolutely necessary; infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; people with an allergic constitution; pregnant women or women who may be pregnant; breastfeeding women; those in whom symptoms of ischemic colitis such as sudden abdominal pain or rectal bleeding appear in relation to the pseudoephedrine component; those who have experienced allergic symptoms to a medicine such as fever, rash, joint pain, asthma or itching; the elderly; and people with a weak body or a high fever.
  • Before taking this medicine, people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma or difficulty urinating, people with persistent or recurrent stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems, and people with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough with excessive phlegm, a cough lasting or recurring for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash or persistent headache should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If the symptoms do not improve after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Children should take it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • Drowsiness may occur while taking it.
  • Avoid driving a car or operating machinery.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, or insomnia occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If shock (anaphylaxis), which rarely may appear immediately after taking the medicine with urticaria, swelling, and chest tightness along with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing, or mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), asthma, liver function disorders such as general fatigue and jaundice, interstitial pneumonia, or symptoms of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome such as sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, or visual disturbance occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take antitussives and expectorants, other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives or oral medicines containing an antihistamine.
  • People who are taking an MAO inhibitor used for the treatment of depression, Parkinson's disease and the like, or who are within 2 weeks of stopping one, should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, people who are being given a diabetes medicine, a gout medicine, an arthritis medicine, an anticoagulant, a steroid or the like should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Patients who are being given a barbiturate, a tricyclic antidepressant or alcohol should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

To prevent motion sickness, take the medicine 30 minutes to 1 hour before boarding: adults and those aged 15 years and over take 1 tablet at a time, those aged 11 years to under 15 years take 2/3 of a tablet at a time, and those aged 8 years to under 11 years take 1/2 of a tablet at a time.   • When administering it to children, do so under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.

  • If rash, congestion causing reddening, itching, urinary difficulty, headache, facial flushing, sensitivity to light, a floating sensation, unsteadiness, thirst (dry mouth), or constipation occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other antiemetics, cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, antihistamines, sedatives, antitussive expectorants, gastrointestinal analgesics and antispasmodics, or the like.

Who should ask first

Those aged 15 years and over and adults take 1 sachet at a time, 3 times a day.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.

  • Very rarely, in patients taking acetaminophen, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily amount of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products that contain acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine and those who have experienced it, people who have had asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age and children under 2 years of age, and people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) or who stopped taking them within the past 2 weeks must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist in the following cases: infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; people with an allergic constitution; people who have had allergic symptoms caused by medicines; people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, edema (puffiness), or gastroduodenal ulcer; elderly people; people who are physically weak or have a high fever; people with persistent or recurring stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems; women who are pregnant or may be pregnant and breastfeeding women; and people who are under treatment by a doctor or dentist.
  • Follow the specified dosage and administration carefully.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness (congestion causing reddening), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema (swelling), light-headedness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis, or, rarely, shock (urticaria, swelling, chest tightness, etc. immediately after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweats, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, in which rash and redness and blisters like burns appear on the skin of the whole body or on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), asthma, liver function disorder (listlessness of the whole body, jaundice), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.), pseudoaldosteronism (decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, a rise in blood pressure or headache, etc.), or myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with antitussives (medicines that stop coughing) and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis (nasal inflammation), motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendinitis, acute gout, dysmenorrhea and bursitis, skeletal muscle disorders (sprain, contusion (bruise), trauma (wound), lumbosacral pain (low back pain)), postoperative pain (aches), migraine, and pain after tooth extraction (pulling out a tooth).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendini

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199902599. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, adults take 1 to 2 tablets (275 to 550 mg) at a time, twice a day (every 12 hours). For acute gout, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 8 hours until the attack subsides. For skeletal muscle disorders, pain after surgery, pain after tooth extraction (having a tooth pulled), dysmenorrhea, tendinitis (inflammation of a tendon), and bursitis (inflammation of the lubricating sac), take 2 tablets (550 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 6 to 8 hours, and do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg). For migraine, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose); if necessary, 1 to 2 more tablets (275 to 550 mg) may be taken a day, and these are taken 30 minutes after the initial dose (the first dose). Do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe renal disorder or severe high blood pressure, patients hypersensitive to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as aspirin, patients who have had asthma, rhinitis (nasal inflammation), nasal polyps, urticaria or an allergic reaction caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors) or those who have experienced them, patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and children aged 2 years or under must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, children, the elderly, those who have experienced peptic ulcer, those who have experienced blood abnormalities, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with liver disorder or those who have experienced it, patients with renal disorder or those who have experienced it, and patients with cardiac dysfunction, high blood pressure, bronchial asthma, systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If an increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke, serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions that may be fatal such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcers, and perforation, rarely shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, a fall in blood pressure, bradycardia (a slow pulse), cold sweat, swelling), PIE syndrome (pulmonary infiltration with eosinophilia: accompanied by fever, wheezing, coughing, and phlegm), urticaria, occasionally hypersensitivity symptoms such as rash or itching, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness), eczema, sweating, purpura (purple spots), photosensitivity, hair loss, redness (turning red from congestion), necrolysis, erythema multiforme (red spots of various shapes), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), urticaria, epidermolysis bullosa, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, fixed drug eruption, exfoliative dermatitis, or rarely blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic (red-blood-cell-destroying) anemia, or reduced platelet function (prolongation of bleeding time) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Occasionally stomach discomfort, stomach pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, or stomatitis (inflammation inside the mouth), and rarely abdominal bloating, black stools, dry mouth, elevated GOT and GPT values, jaundice, hepatitis, kidney disorder, nephritis, hematuria, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, proteinuria (urine containing protein), renal failure, ringing in the ears, hearing impairment, visual impairment, swelling, difficulty breathing, palpitations (a pounding heart), myasthenia (muscle weakness), congestive heart failure, eosinophilic pneumonia, anaphylactoid reactions, menstrual disorders, chills (feeling cold and shivering) and fever, vasculitis, high blood sugar, or low blood sugar may occur.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics or naproxen derivatives, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with hydantoin antiepileptics, sulfonamides, sulfonylurea hypoglycemic agents, propranolol and other blockers, ACE inhibitors (such as captopril), loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics, probenecid, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (blood-clotting inhibitors) (such as warfarin), zidovudine, or new quinolone antibiotics (such as enoxacin).

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, heart failure, or high blood pressure, patients with bronchial asthma, patients with asthma, urticaria, or allergy caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics or those who have experienced it, patients being treated for pain before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, and pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women should not take this medicine.

  • If rarely shock (difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, etc.), aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, decreased platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms of unknown frequency (DRESS syndrome), acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, induction of an asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, or purpura occurs, or occasionally rash or itching, or rarely loss of vision, visual disturbances such as scotoma, aseptic meningitis, acute renal failure, oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN or blood creatinine, or hyperkalemia occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not use this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when using it together with glucocorticoids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, the combined use of diuretics and antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors, furosemide, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, or coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin, etc.).

  • Before taking this medicine, infants (newborns) and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, people with an allergic constitution, people who have experienced allergic symptoms caused by medicines (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), or difficulty urinating (passing urine), elderly people, people who are physically weak or who have a high fever, people with persistent or recurring gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, patients with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that persists or recurs for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or a persistent headache, and children under 2 years of age should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after 5 to 6 doses, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • When administering it to children, do so under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness (congested and reddened skin), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema (swelling), difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, rarely shock (urticaria, edema (swelling) and chest tightness together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat and difficulty breathing, etc.), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) (when severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness (congested and reddened skin) and blistering like a burn, appear on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), asthma, liver function disorder (generalized listlessness, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turning yellow), etc.), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, breathlessness, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.), symptoms of ischemic colitis (sudden abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, etc.), or posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizure, visual disturbance, etc.) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussives (which stop coughing) and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis (nasal inflammation), motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).

  • Patients who are given barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.

At a glance

Category

How it works

This drug is used for reducing fever when fever occurs due to acute upper respiratory tract infection.

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201305834. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 6 months and over take 0.4 to 0.6 mL/kg (5 to 7 mg/kg) at a time as needed, at intervals of 4 to 6 hours, not exceeding a maximum of 4 times a day (28 mg/kg). For children weighing 30 kg or less, do not exceed a maximum of 25 mL (300 mg) a day. If the body weight is known it is more appropriate to give the dose based on body weight, so refer to the approved labelling for the recommended doses by age group.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious, potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, or those with a history of these, people who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or an allergic reaction to aspirin or another non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesic (including COX-2 inhibitors), patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, and women who are pregnant or may be pregnant or are breastfeeding must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you have a history of peptic ulcer, blood abnormalities or a history of them, a bleeding tendency (platelet dysfunction may occur), liver disorder or a history of it, kidney disorder or a history of it, cardiac insufficiency, high blood pressure, a history of hypersensitivity, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, are elderly or a child, or have stomach cancer.
  • Considering the importance of the medication, either stop breastfeeding or stop the medication.
  • Dizziness or fatigue may occur after taking this medicine, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • When taking it long term for an acute condition, keep it to within 5 days as a rule.

Possible side effects

  • If shock (difficulty breathing, a drop in blood pressure, etc.), blood disorders such as aplastic anaemia, haemolytic anaemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), or eosinophilia occur, or peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (oculomucocutaneous syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), induction of an asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purpura, occasionally rash or itching, rarely visual disturbances such as loss of vision or scotoma, aseptic meningitis, acute renal failure, oliguria, haematuria, proteinuria, a rise in BUN or blood creatinine, or hyperkalaemia occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Occasionally loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhoea, or stomach discomfort may occur; very rarely thirst, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, or constipation; rarely jaundice, a rise in GOT, GPT, or AL-P, hearing loss, tinnitus, taste disturbance, a drop in blood pressure, a rise in blood pressure, palpitations, reduced urine output, generalised oedema and the accompanying shortness of breath, listlessness, or acute pulmonary oedema; occasionally periorbital oedema; and very rarely malaise, fever, or nosebleed.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with glucocorticoids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, diuretics, antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors, furosemide, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or low-dose aspirin.

Those aged 15 years and over take 1 sachet (20 mL), those aged 11 years to under 15 years take 2/3 of a sachet, those aged 7 years to under 11 years take 1/2 of a sachet, those aged 3 years to under 7 years take 1/3 of a sachet, and those aged 2 years to under 3 years take 1/4 of a sachet, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when they take this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine or with such a history, people who have had asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants (newborns) under 3 months of age, and patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you are a child aged 3 months and over but under 2 years, an infant or a child under 15 years of age who is infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, a person with an allergic constitution or a history of allergy to medicines, a person with liver, kidney, heart, or thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), or difficulty urinating (passing urine), an elderly person, a person who is physically weak or who has a high fever, a person with persistent or recurring gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain or with ulcers or bleeding problems, a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant, a breastfeeding woman, or a person with symptoms such as smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that persists or recurs for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or a persistent headache.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • When administering it to children, do so under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • If symptoms do not improve after 5 to 6 doses, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rash and redness (reddening of the skin), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling (puffiness), difficulty urinating (passing urine), persistent or severe thirst, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia; shock symptoms (urticaria, edema, and chest tightness right after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing); Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome); toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome: severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness and blistering like burns); asthma; general lethargy; jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turn yellow); interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.); symptoms of ischemic colitis related to the pseudoephedrine component (sudden abdominal pain, rectal bleeding); or posterior reversible encephalopathy and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, visual disturbances, etc.).

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussives and expectorants (cough and phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis [nasal inflammation], motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).

  • People who are being given other medicines such as barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants and alcohol, diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, or steroids should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Who should ask first

How to take it

Adults and children aged 8 years and over take 20 to 40 mL (1 to 2 sachets) a day, based on a package unit of 1 sachet (20 mL). Depending on the symptoms, children in particular may take 20 mL (1 sachet) every two days. Dissolve 20 mL (1 sachet) of this medicine in water to make 50 mL and take it. It is recommended to take it in the morning. Children from 6 months to 7 years of age, based on a package unit of 1 sachet (8 mL), take 8 mL (1 sachet) a day at 6 months to 1 year of age, 8 to 16 mL (1 to 2 sachets) a day at 1 to 4 years of age, and 16 to 32 mL (2 to 4 sachets) a day at 4 to 7 years of age. When 1 sachet (8 mL) a day is taken, take it in the morning, and when more than 1 sachet (8 mL) a day is taken, divide it between morning and evening. Dissolve 8 mL (1 sachet) of this medicine in water to make 50 mL and take it.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients with inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, etc.) or toxic megacolon, by patients with intestinal perforation or at risk of intestinal perforation, by patients who have or are suspected of having intestinal obstruction, by patients with intestinal stricture, or by patients with abdominal pain of unknown cause.

  • In children, do not give this medicine for 3 months or more, and do not give this medicine for a long period without the judgment of a doctor.

  • In adults, if abdominal pain and abdominal distension, diarrhea or nausea appears, if vomiting, urgent defecation or fecal incontinence uncommonly appears, if electrolyte disturbance (hyponatremia, hypokalemia, etc.), dehydration or erythema appears at an unknown frequency, or if a hypersensitivity reaction (itching, rash, facial edema, angioedema, urticaria, anaphylactic shock, etc.) very rarely appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg at a time, 3-4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be administered. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30-40 mg per kg of body weight at a time, 3 to 4 times a day. For mild to moderate pain and colds, adults take 200-400 mg at a time, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased appropriately according to age and symptoms. Children 11 to 14 years of age take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 12.5 mL) at a time, children 7 to 10 years of age take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 mL) at a time, children 3 to 6 years of age take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 mL) at a time, and children 1 to 2 years of age take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 mL) at a time, 3 to 4 times a day.

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood abnormalities, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, patients who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, breastfeeding women, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

How to take it

Children 6 months of age and older take 0.4 to 0.6 mL/kg (5 to 7 mg/kg) at a time, as needed at intervals of 4 to 6 hours, not exceeding a maximum of 4 times a day (28 mg/kg). For children weighing 30 kg or less, do not exceed a maximum of 25 mL (300 mg) a day. If the body weight is known, dosing according to body weight is more appropriate, so refer to the approved product information for the recommended dose by age group.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious, potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe heart failure, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, people who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients being treated for pain before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, and pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with or with a history of blood abnormalities, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with or with a history of liver disorder, patients with or with a history of kidney disorder, patients with heart failure or high blood pressure, people who have experienced hypersensitivity, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease, patients with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, the elderly, children, patients with stomach cancer, and people who take low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If it is taken long term, as a rule limit this to 5 days or less.

Possible side effects

  • If rarely shock (difficulty breathing, fall in blood pressure, etc.), blood disorders such as aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time) or eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), induction of an asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purpura, occasionally rash or itching, or rarely visual disturbances such as loss of vision or dimming of vision, aseptic meningitis, acute renal failure, oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN or blood creatinine, or hyperkalemia occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If occasionally loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea or stomach discomfort, or very rarely dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal distension or constipation, or rarely jaundice, elevated GOT, GPT or ALP, hearing loss, tinnitus, taste abnormality, fall in blood pressure, rise in blood pressure, palpitations, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath or listlessness, acute pulmonary edema, occasionally periorbital edema, or very rarely malaise, fever or nosebleed occur, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not use this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, aspirin or high-dose methotrexate.
  • If used together with glucocorticoids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, a combination of a diuretic and an antihypertensive, ACE inhibitors, furosemide, lithium, low-dose methotrexate or coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin, etc.), consult a doctor or pharmacist.

When pain makes it difficult to sleep, adults take 1 to 2 capsules at a time, once a day before bedtime. Including this medicine, do not exceed 1,200 mg of ibuprofen and 75 mg of diphenhydramine in 24 hours. Leave an interval of at least 4 hours between doses.   • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant, breastfeeding women, children under 15 years of age, patients with or with a history of gastrointestinal ulcer or bleeding, patients with or with a history of bronchial asthma, patients with difficulty breathing due to asthma attacks, emphysema, or chronic bronchitis, patients with or with a history of hypersensitivity to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions, patients with severe blood abnormalities, liver impairment, cardiac insufficiency, or high blood pressure, patients with glaucoma, lower urinary tract obstructive disease such as benign prostatic hyperplasia, convulsive disorders such as epilepsy, or pheochromocytoma, and patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery must not take this medicine.

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for the relief of pain from headache, toothache, pain after tooth extraction, sore throat, earache

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202500756. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those 15 years and older take 3 sachets at a time, those 11 years and older but under 15 years take 2 sachets at a time, those 7 years and older but under 11 years take 3/2 sachet at a time, those 3 years and older but under 7 years take 1 sachet at a time, and those 2 years and older but under 3 years take 3/4 sachet at a time, 3 times a day, avoiding an empty stomach.   • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of hypersensitivity appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.

  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine and those who have experienced it, people who have had asthma when taking this medicine or its ingredients, other antipyretic analgesics, or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.

  • Follow the specified dosage and administration carefully.
  • When it is given to children, give it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rash, redness, itching, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, dizziness, edema, high anion gap metabolic acidosis; rarely shock symptoms (urticaria, edema, and chest tightness right after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing); Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome); toxic epidermal necrolysis (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness and blistering like burns appearing on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes); asthma; general lethargy; or jaundice.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other antipyretic analgesics, cold medicines or sedatives.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.
  • If you take it together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol or flucloxacillin, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used to inhibit thrombus formation in myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction, and unstable angina, to inhibit thrombus formation after coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) or percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA), and to reduce cardiovascular risk in high-risk patients (patients with multiple risk factors such as a family history of ischemic heart disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obesity, and diabetes).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to inhibit thrombus formation in myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction, and unstable angina,

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201603416. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults take 1 tablet as 1 dose, 1 time a day. Since this medicine is an enteric-coated tablet, it may be taken before meals with plenty of water.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or to other salicylate preparations, analgesics, anti-inflammatory agents or antirheumatic agents, patients with peptic ulcer or aspirin-induced asthma or a history of it, patients with hemophilia, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency or a tendency to bleed, patients receiving concomitant methotrexate at doses of 15 mg or more per week (15 mg/week), and pregnant women in the third trimester must not take this medicine.
  • Do not take this medicine during the first and second trimesters of pregnancy unless it is absolutely necessary.
  • Before using this medicine, patients with kidney disorder, cardiovascular circulatory dysfunction (renal vascular disease, congestive heart failure, fluid depletion, major surgery, sepsis or major bleeding events, etc.), liver disorder, impaired cardiac function or bronchial asthma, patients before surgery, young children aged 3 years or under, elderly people, patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, patients with Reye's syndrome, patients aged 14 years or under with chickenpox or influenza infection, and patients with gout should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Because there is a risk of bleeding, tell your doctor that you are taking this medicine if you are going to have surgery (including dental surgery).
  • Take care not to damage the enteric coating of this medicine.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms (e.g. difficulty breathing, generalized flushing, angioedema, hives), asthma attacks, hypersensitivity (erythema, itching, nasal congestion, cardiac and respiratory disorders, and sometimes rash, swelling, hives, rhinitis-like symptoms, conjunctivitis), rarely toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), skin-mucosa-eye syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), exfoliative dermatitis, rarely aplastic anemia, anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), ringing in the ears, deafness, dizziness, headache, agitation, rarely liver disorder, or very rarely temporary liver damage, renal impairment, acute renal failure, hyperventilation, metabolic acidosis, an excessive drop in body temperature, collapse, or coldness of the limbs occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Loss of appetite, heartburn, stomach pain, nausea, and vomiting may occur.

Interactions

  • Other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics and salicylate preparations, and methotrexate at doses of 15 mg or more per week (15 mg/week), must not be used together with this medicine, because concomitant use may increase bleeding or reduce kidney function.
  • People taking anticoagulants, some non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as ibuprofen and naproxen, thrombolytics, other platelet aggregation inhibitors, hemostatics, antidiabetic agents (insulin preparations, tolbutamide, etc.), uricosuric agents (benzbromarone, probenecid), thiazide diuretics, lithium preparations, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, digoxin, systemically acting adrenocortical hormone preparations (excluding hydrocortisone used as replacement therapy for Addison's disease), angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, or valproic acid preparations should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not mix this medicine with alkaline preparations (for example, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium carbonate) or with preparations that easily absorb moisture.
  • Concomitant use with alcohol increases damage to the gastrointestinal mucosa, and the synergistic effect of this medicine and alcohol may prolong bleeding time.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over and adults take 2 capsules at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. Those aged 8 years and over but under 15 years take 1 capsule at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine or with such a history, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants (newborns) under 3 months of age, and patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants (newborns) and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, people with an allergic constitution, people who have experienced allergic symptoms caused by medicines (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), or difficulty urinating (passing urine), elderly people, people who are physically weak or who have a high fever, people with persistent or recurring gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, patients with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that persists or recurs for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or a persistent headache, and children under 2 years of age should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
